title: First communion (1884)
hookLine: Thérèse calls her first communion a kiss of love; how much does a child need to understand first?
tomorrow: what if everything you do starts to feel like a sin?

lines: A WHITE SUIT, A SHEET CAKE.
HOW MUCH MUST A CHILD UNDERSTAND?
cards: A little kid in a white suit, tugging at the collar. A grandmother holding her phone up through the whole Mass. A sheet cake waiting at home.
Thérèse, writing years later about her own first communion, reaches for a word nobody expects from a child: a kiss. A kiss of love.
And her story touches a question Catholics have weighed for a long time: how much does a child need to understand first?

teach.b: First, her morning. Pauline, writing from Carmel, made her a little book to prepare, and day by day Thérèse gathered small sacrifices and acts of love, the way you'd gather flowers. Then it came.
She felt loved, she says, and she answered: I love you, and I give myself to you forever.
It was no longer a look between two, she writes, but a fusion. Thérèse had disappeared like a drop of water in the ocean. She cried, and grown-ups thought she missed her mother.
No, she says. Joy. Behind it is Jesus's promise, in the Douay-Rheims: "He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, abideth in me, and I in him."

teach.h: PREPARE LONG, OR DON'T MAKE THEM WAIT?
teach.b: One says: prepare long and carefully, so a child grasps what she receives.
Thérèse's own loving preparation shows what that can give. The other is Pope Pius the Tenth's.
Children shouldn't be kept waiting, he wrote. Once they reach the age of reason and can tell this bread from ordinary bread, they may receive; full understanding isn't required, and it grows after.
Both sides want the same thing: a child meeting Christ, not passing a test.

how: Catholic children prepare in their parish for first communion and receive it at Mass, often with their families present.

o: receiving the Eucharist for the very first time
a child's first time serving at the altar
the first time a child goes to confession

p: small sacrifices and acts of love
lost in the ocean: no longer two
the age of reason is enough

s: a child must fully understand the Eucharist before first communion
Pius X said the age of reason is enough: telling this bread from ordinary bread.
Thérèse described that morning as a fusion: no longer two
like a drop of water lost in the ocean.
Thérèse's tears that day were for her mother
the grown-ups thought so. she says they were tears of joy.

games.q: your aunt thinks first communion should wait until kids are older and really get it. you lean the other way. what's her strongest point?
o: a long, loving preparation, like Thérèse's, helps a child know what she receives.
younger children can't be loved by God in the same way.
Church rules say a child must understand everything first.
games.why: that's the best case for waiting, and Thérèse's own preparation shows its beauty. Pius X answered that the age of reason is enough. both want a meeting, not a test.

practice: Count on your fingers three times you were welcomed completely somewhere: a table, a team, a church, a friend's kitchen. If you made a first communion, let it be one of them.
If you pray, you can rest in John's words: abideth in me, and I in him.

wordCard.voice: First communion. Receiving the Eucharist for the first time, which Thérèse called a kiss of love.

carryVoice: Keep this close: a kiss of love, the welcome before any rule. Goodnight for now.
